paras: The attempted removal of a wounded Black soldier from a Texas sleeping car was an incident in early 1919 in which white passengers objected to a Black veteran riding in a sleeper on a federally operated train. The objectors stood aside after the soldier's white lieutenant said he would be removed only over the officer's dead body. The Dallas Express used the incident in an editorial against Jim Crow and "white supremacy."

According to the Dallas Express, the soldier was returning from the Western Front, where he had been "almost mortally wounded," to his home in Tyler, Texas. The paper described him as "a chocolate brown" and said he had ridden in a sleeper under army instruction, with a white lieutenant as his caretaker.

The editorial placed the incident "only the other day at Texrkana or a few miles out," on a train operated by the federal government. When the train reached Imperial, Texas, by the same account, some white people objected to his continuing in the sleeper, and it seemed he would be removed by force if necessary. The lieutenant then told the objectors that the soldier would not be removed except over his dead body, and the objectors stood aside. Neither the soldier nor the lieutenant is named, and no one is reported injured.

The only report found is a paragraph in an unsigned editorial column of the Dallas Express on 15 March 1919, under the heading "Physician Heal Thyself." The column called the objectors "upholsters of 'white supremacy'" and praised "the wounded hero and his gallant protector." It argued that "the enemies of America do not all live in Germany" and contrasted the episode with President Wilson preaching democracy in Europe while it went unpracticed at home. No other coverage in the Black press was found.
The account's geography is unclear: it places the train at or near Texarkana but names Imperial, Texas, as the point where the objection was made.
